title: Building this portfolio with an AI coding agent
summary: What worked for me when pairing with an AI coding agent: small steps, a review pass on each one, and testing before committing.
content:
This portfolio is coming together with the help of an AI coding agent, and the part that matters most is not the generating - it is the reviewing. I give the agent one small step at a time, and every step is reviewed and tested before it gets committed.

Working in small steps makes mistakes cheap. A review step caught a bug in the email validation: the whitespace rule had to be fixed so an email with a space in it is rejected, and that fix landed as its own tiny commit instead of hiding inside a big batch of changes. Because each step was small, the bug was easy to see and easy to describe.

The habit I am trying to build is simple: one commit tells one small story, and I can explain every line in it. If I cannot, that is a sign I need to slow down and read more carefully.

title: Why I validate forms on the server
summary: Browser validation is a courtesy, not a guarantee. The server has to be the one that decides what data is acceptable.
content:
It is tempting to think validation lives in the browser: the form highlights the bad field, the user fixes it, done. But anyone can call your API directly with curl, so whatever checks only exist in the browser do not actually protect your data.

That is why the contact form on this site validates on the server. The rules live in one shared module, and both ways in - the React server action and the JSON API route - call the same function. There is exactly one copy of the rules, so the two entry points cannot drift apart.

My rule of thumb: the client can validate early to help the user, but the server always validates again before saving, because the server is the only place that is impossible to skip.
